nameStory: Despite its name, Scotch broom isn't exclusively Scottish - it's native throughout western and central Europe. The 'broom' part comes from its traditional use: people would bundle the tough, flexible branches together to make actual brooms for sweeping. In Scotland, it was so commonly used for this purpose that the plant became forever linked with the country in people's minds.
description: Scotch broom is a deciduous shrub that grows 3-6 feet tall with an upright, somewhat spindly appearance. It's covered in bright yellow, pea-like flowers in late spring and early summer that are hard to miss. The plant has small, oval leaves and distinctive green, ridged stems that remain visible even after the leaves drop. Originally from Europe, it has spread widely across New England and is considered an invasive species in many areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers shaped like pea blossoms, about 3/4 inch long, covering the branches in late spring. Each flower has the classic 'butterfly' shape of legume flowers with a large upper petal and smaller side petals that smell faintly sweet.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctive bright green, ridged stems that feel firm and slightly waxy to the touch. These angular, grooved branches stay green year-round and are easily visible in winter, giving the plant a somewhat artificial, plastic-like appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves that are often grouped in threes, feeling smooth and somewhat thick. Many stems appear nearly leafless, especially as the season progresses, making the green branches more prominent than the foliage.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, somewhat scraggly shrub with many ascending branches that create an open, airy appearance. Often forms dense colonies along roadsides and disturbed areas, with multiple stems arising from the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened, dark brown seed pods about 1-2 inches long that split open with an audible 'pop' on hot summer days. The pods turn from green to black and contain several small, hard seeds that rattle when shaken.

habitat: Look for Scotch broom along roadsides, in disturbed soils, abandoned lots, and forest edges throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils and full sun, often establishing itself on highway cuts and slopes where it was originally planted for erosion control. You'll commonly find it mixed with other weedy shrubs and invasive plants in areas that have been cleared or disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early and the spectacular yellow flower display begins in late spring, typically May into early June. This is when the plant is most noticeable and easiest to identify from a distance.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and seed pods develop, turning from green to brown. The plant may look somewhat scraggly as leaves become less prominent and the green stems dominate the appearance.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen to dark brown or black and begin splitting open. Some leaves may yellow and drop, making the evergreen stems even more obvious.
seasonality.winter: The bright green, ridged stems remain the most distinctive feature, creating an almost artificial-looking shrub skeleton. This is when the plant's unusual stem structure is most apparent.

funFact: Scotch broom seed pods explode on hot, sunny days with an audible popping sound, flinging seeds up to 15 feet away - you can actually hear a patch of broom 'crackling' like popcorn as you walk by on a warm summer afternoon!
confusionNotes: The bright green, ridged stems that stay green all winter are unique among New England shrubs, making this plant hard to confuse with anything else. In flower, the masses of yellow pea-like blooms are distinctive, though individual flowers might be confused with other legumes - but no other shrub in our region produces such a spectacular yellow display.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'Scotch' broom, this plant is considered a serious invasive species in New England and much of North America. It was originally planted for erosion control and ornamental purposes but has escaped cultivation. The seeds remain viable in soil for up to 10 years, making established populations very difficult to eliminate.
compareHints: Scotch broom is the only species in the broom genus (Cytisus) commonly found in New England. Among other legume shrubs, it's easily distinguished by its bright green, ridged stems that remain prominent year-round and its spectacular mass of yellow flowers. Other yellow-flowered legumes in our region are typically herbaceous plants rather than woody shrubs.
